title: Arts4All Diwali and Navaratri Festival Draws 2,000 to Queens Unisphere
excerpt: The free World's Fair festival at Flushing Meadows Corona Park paired a light ceremony and parade with vegetarian food, rangoli, henna and Garba — a celebration built as much on service as on festivity.
body:
• About 2,000 people gathered at the Unisphere in Flushing Meadows Corona Park on October 10 for the Arts4All Foundation's World's Fair Diwali and Navaratri Festival and Parade, according to the South Asian Herald.
  • The free, family event ran from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. and combined a light ceremony and parade with food, arts and crafts, games, and live music and dance.
  • Food is central to the festival's service ethos: the annual celebration's format includes free vegetarian meals shared with attendees and underserved New Yorkers.
  • The festival followed the foundation's September 20 gala honouring New York leaders, and pays tribute to the 1964 World's Fair held at the same site.

About 2,000 people turned out at the Unisphere in Queens on October 10 for the Arts4All Foundation's World's Fair Diwali and Navaratri Festival and Parade, according to the South Asian Herald — a free afternoon of light ceremonies, Garba and dance, arts and crafts, and shared food in front of one of New York's most recognisable landmarks.

The festival ran from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. at Flushing Meadows Corona Park and was open to all ages, the Arts4All Foundation's event page shows, with a light ceremony, a parade, games and live music and dance performances. In Queens — routinely described by its own organisers as the "World's Borough" — the celebration drew South Asian and Indo-Caribbean families alongside neighbours from across the city's communities.

Food as the festival's language of service

Eating together is not a side attraction at this festival; it is part of its founding idea. The foundation's own listing promises "delicious food" as a core part of the afternoon, and coverage of the annual celebration by the Queens Gazette documents the format the festival has built its name on: more than 1,100 pure vegetarian cooked meals served free to attendees and underserved New Yorkers, alongside toys, balloons and gold chocolate coins for children. In the festival's established format, the meals have been provided by Navdeep Singh, owner of Punjabi Dhaba in Richmond Hill, Queens.

That pairing — a religious festival run as an act of public service — is deliberate. Arts4All is a human-rights organisation, and its founder, Dr. Sumita SenGupta, frames Diwali and Navaratri as holidays that should move people to be, in her words, "a light and positive force of good" in their community. Rangoli artwork, henna, face painting, yoga and a Diya light aarti have all featured in the annual programme, with the evening parade circling the Unisphere as diyas are lit at sunset.

A gala set the stage

This year's festival followed the foundation's World's Fair Diwali and Navaratri Gala on September 20, where it honoured elected officials, doctors and community leaders, the South Asian Herald reported. Honorees included New York State Comptroller Thomas P. DiNapoli, Rep. Laura A. Gillen, and physicians Dr. Sudhir M. Parikh and Dr. Sudha S. Parikh, and the evening featured Bharatanatyam performances, Hindi songs and a Garba dance contest before a diya lighting ceremony.

The Unisphere setting carries its own meaning. The annual festival pays tribute to the 1964 New York World's Fair, which was held on the same grounds, and the celebration also keeps alive a family tradition: elected officials at past editions have recalled that one of Queens' first community Diwali gatherings was held more than 50 years ago in the Flushing apartment of the late Uma SenGupta, Dr. SenGupta's mother, with about twenty people. The gathering her daughter now runs draws thousands.

Why it matters beyond one afternoon

More than seven million Americans observe Diwali and Navaratri, and New York's public celebrations have become a fixture of the city's autumn calendar. For second-generation families, a festival at a public landmark — free, outdoors, and built around food and dance rather than tickets — is often the easiest way to hand the holidays to children growing up American. For the wider city, it is South Asian and Indo-Caribbean culture presented on civic ground, at civic scale.

What comes next

The festival anchors the foundation's autumn season, which continues through the Diwali period with community events across Queens. Families who missed the Unisphere celebration can follow the foundation's event listings for the next edition — registration for this year's festival filled in advance, and the afternoon remains free.
